The Sea Inside the Stone

I have always been secretly jealous of stones.

Not for their durability, though that is impressive. Not for their silence, though I crave that sometimes. I am jealous of how completely a stone commits to being exactly where it is. It doesn't worry about where it should have been, or daydream about the riverbed two valleys over. It is entirely itself, entirely present, sun-warm on one side and moss-cool on the other. Humans, by contrast, are almost never where we are. Our bodies stand in kitchens and train stations and grocery aisles, but our minds are somewhere else entirely — replaying a conversation from 2014, rehearsing a conversation for 2027, trying to remember if we left the stove on.

So if I'm going to write freely, with no assignment and no destination, I want to start there: with the problem and the privilege of being a creature that lives half in the world and half in its own head. And I want to follow that thread wherever it wants to go, for as long as it will.

### 1. The Universe Is Made of Leftovers

Look up at night, far away from city lights, and the sky doesn't look like a place. It looks like a memory. That's not poetry, it's physics. The light from that star left its surface when mammoths were still walking the earth. The light from that smudgy galaxy left before there were mammoths, before there were trees, before there was dirt. You are not seeing the universe as it is; you are seeing it as it was, layered like old paint on a wall.

Everything we are made of is a leftover, too. The iron in your blood, the calcium in your teeth, the potassium that fires every heartbeat — none of it could be made in the Big Bang. The early universe was too hot and too simple. It only knew how to make hydrogen and helium, the two lightest elements, like a child who only knows how to draw with two crayons.

All the rest was forged later, in the violent second act. Stars lived and died. And in dying, they did something extraordinary. A star like our sun will end quietly, puffing off its outer layers like a dandelion clock. But a star much bigger than our sun dies in a supernova, and for a few seconds, it outshines an entire galaxy. In that impossible furnace, atoms are slammed together into new forms. Carbon, oxygen, gold, uranium. Then the explosion scatters them across the dark like seeds.

So the ring on your finger, the screen you are reading this on, the air in your lungs — all of it is stardust that got lucky. Carl Sagan said it and it became a poster, but it remains literally true and still under-appreciated. We are not *in* the universe. We are a way for the leftover pieces of dead stars to briefly assemble themselves into a shape that can wonder where it came from.

I think about that when I wash dishes sometimes. The water running over my hands is older than the sun. The hydrogen atoms in it were made 13.8 billion years ago. They have been ocean and cloud and glacier and blood and tears, over and over again. My hands are just the latest place they happen to be passing through. That should make me feel small, but it doesn't. It makes me feel like a custodian. For a few decades I get to borrow this handful of ancient atoms and arrange them into something that can laugh and make soup and be kind to strangers. I should try to be a good custodian.

### 2. The Invention of Memory

We talk about memory as if it were a filing cabinet. We "store" memories, "retrieve" them, "lose" them. But that metaphor is completely wrong and it quietly breaks our hearts, because we blame ourselves when the cabinet fails us.

Memory is not a recording. It is a reconstruction. Every time you remember your childhood kitchen, you are not playing back a video. You are rebuilding the kitchen from scraps in the workshop of the present moment. Your brain keeps the smell of the cleaner under the sink, the color of the linoleum, the sound the drawer made when it stuck — but not as a single file. As a scattered constellation of associations. When you recall it, you reassemble it, and the present leaks in. Your current mood, what someone told you yesterday, the story you've told about that kitchen a dozen times before — all of it edits the reconstruction.

That is why two siblings can grow up in the same house and remember two completely different childhoods, and both be telling the truth. That is why an old memory can suddenly feel different after years of feeling the same. You are not lying to yourself. You are just rebuilding the same house with slightly different materials each time.

And yet, some things remain shockingly stable. I can still remember the exact way my grandmother's hands looked when she peeled an apple in one long, unbroken spiral. I can remember the sound of the hallway heater clicking on in the apartment I lived in when I was seven. Not important things, not lessons or morals. Just textures. The brain is not a historian; it is a hoarder. It keeps what it found beautiful or strange or frightening, often without asking permission.

There is a kind of freedom in understanding this. If memory is an act of imagination, then nostalgia is not just longing for the past. It is longing for a past that never quite existed in the form we miss it. And that means we are free — obligated, even — to be more deliberate about the memories we are making now. Not by taking more photos, necessarily, but by paying more attention while the present is still happening. Attention is the only way we tell our future remembering selves what is worth keeping.

The poet Mary Oliver wrote, "Attention is the beginning of devotion." Neuroscience would agree. What you attend to, you encode more deeply. So to live a memorable life is not to have a more dramatic life. It is to have a more *attentive* one. To notice the way light falls across the table at 4 p.m. in October. To listen, really listen, when someone tells you how their day was, even when the story is not exciting. Those are the scraps your future self will have to work with when it tries to rebuild what it meant to be alive right now.

### 3. The City Inside Your Pocket

For most of human history, if you wanted to know something, you had to ask a person who knew it, or walk to where the answer lived. Knowledge had a geography. It lived in the elder, in the library, in the temple. If the elder died before passing it on, it was gone. If the library burned, it was gone.

Now we carry a rectangle of glass in our pockets that contains, in a very real sense, almost everything we have ever written down. The sum of human knowledge, the entire archive, plus a near-infinite supply of nonsense and cruelty and cat videos, all flattened into the same glowing feed. It is a miracle so complete we have already become bored of it. We complain about the miracle when it loads slowly.

This has rewired us in ways we are still too close to see clearly. But one change feels obvious: we have outsourced not just memory, but wonder.

When I was a child, if I wondered why the moon sometimes comes out during the day, that question would sit with me for days. It would itch. I would carry it to school, turn it over, maybe ask a teacher who would half-remember an answer about orbits. The question had weight because it had to travel to find its answer.

Now the interval between wondering and knowing has collapsed to three seconds and two thumb swipes. Which is extraordinary — and it also means we rarely *live* inside a question anymore. We don't dwell in not-knowing. And not-knowing is where all the interesting things grow. Curiosity, humility, awe. The ability to hold two conflicting ideas without immediately picking a winner.

The internet did not make us less curious. It made us less patient with our curiosity. We want resolution instantly. But some questions deserve to be slow-cooked. "What should I do with my life?" cannot be Googled, though many of us try. "Am I a good person?" "Why did that friendship end?" "What does this grief want from me?" Those questions will not be answered by information. They will be answered, if at all, by lived time.

I don't want to be a Luddite about this. I love having a map of every street on earth in my pocket. I love that I can video-call my friend who moved to another continent. But I have started practicing a small, private discipline: when a beautiful, useless question appears — why do crows collect shiny things, what makes the sea smell like the sea, how did my great-grandparents meet — I try to wait 24 hours before looking it up. I let the question keep me company for a day. I notice how it changes the way I see the world while it is still unanswered. Often, by the time I finally look it up, the answer matters less than the day I spent wondering.

### 4. How To Disappear Completely and Still Be Found

There is a fantasy almost everyone has had at least once: to disappear. Not to die, but to slip the context that holds you in place. To leave your name and your inbox and your reputation behind and become an anonymous person in a new town where no one knows your history. To walk into a cafe where no one expects anything from you and just be a person drinking coffee.

In the past, you could actually do that. You could get on a train, get off three states away, get a job washing dishes, rent a room, become someone else by degrees. Now disappearance is much harder. Your name is tethered to you by data. Your face is in a hundred databases. Your old life will find you through an algorithm that suggests you as "someone you may know."

And yet people still manage to disappear in a more meaningful way, without ever leaving home. They disappear by changing what they pay attention to.

You can disappear from an argument by refusing to replay it in your head for the hundredth time. You can disappear from the frantic economy of status by not checking how many people liked what you made. You can disappear from a family myth that says you are "the difficult one" or "the responsible one" by quietly, over years, acting in a way that makes the myth no longer fit. You don't announce it. You just live until the old story about you becomes obviously false.

Perhaps the opposite fantasy is equally strong: to be fully found. To be known, accurately and tenderly, by another person who sees not just your curated surface but the tangled, contradictory underside — and stays. We spend so much of life managing how we are perceived that the moments of being truly perceived feel almost holy. A friend who remembers the small thing you mentioned weeks ago. A stranger on a bus who catches your eye and smiles exactly when you needed it. A therapist, a lover, a child, who sees you without flinching.

These two desires — to disappear and to be found — sound opposite, but they are not. They are the same desire for sovereignty. *I want to be able to choose when I am seen.*

Modern life often steals that choice. We are seen constantly, by cameras and trackers and timelines, but rarely *perceived*. We are visible but not known. The cure is not to hide. It is to seek out the few places and people where perception is still slow and human. A long walk without a phone. A conversation with no agenda. A room where you can be boring together without performing.

I have come to believe that privacy is not about secrecy. It is about having an interior life that is not for sale. A garden with a fence around it, not because the flowers are shameful, but because the fence lets them grow without being trampled. Everyone needs a place that is not being watched, even if that place is only inside your own head for ten minutes a day.

### 5. A Letter to the Future That Will Not Remember Us

If you are reading this in fifty years, hello. Or in a hundred years, hello anyway. I don't know what words will still exist when you find this. Maybe English will sound as strange to you as Old English does to me. Maybe you will be reading this through a translation layer that smooths my clumsy sentences into something more elegant than I deserve.

I want to tell you what it was like here, in 2026, in the middle of everything.

It was loud. Not just audibly loud, though cities were loud. But informationally loud. Everyone could speak to everyone all the time, and everyone did. This made us feel both powerful and powerless. We could organize a protest in a day and also feel completely unable to stop a war on the other side of the planet that we watched live on our phones. We argued a lot, often about things that would not matter in a month, because arguing was a way to feel like we were doing something.

It was anxious. We knew more about the planet's fever than any generation before us, and we knew we were late to fix it. Many of us carried a low, humming grief about the future, even while we made dinner and fell in love and went to the movies. We held two truths at once: that the world was burning and that the world was still exquisitely beautiful, and we did not know how to hold them without feeling torn.

It was also, unexpectedly, tender. Because we were so aware of how fragile everything was, many of us became more gentle with each other in small, unrecorded ways. We adopted old dogs. We wrote letters by hand again, as an antidote to speed. We learned to bake bread not because we needed bread but because we needed to watch something rise slowly and predictably for once. We said "I love you" more easily, because we had learned — from a pandemic, from fires, from losing people through screens — that the time to say it is always shorter than we think.

If you have photographs of us, we probably look distracted. We are staring at our little rectangles. I'm sorry about that. We were trying to connect through them, and sometimes we did, but often we were just doomscrolling, which is a word that will hopefully be obsolete for you. It meant compulsively reading bad news until our nervous systems buzzed.

If you have our art, I hope some of it survived. We made so much of it, even though machines had started to make art too. Or perhaps *because* machines had started to make it. We needed to prove, mostly to ourselves, that a human hand still mattered. That imperfection was a signature, not an error.

Here is what I wish for you, whoever you are: I wish you have clean air without having to check an app to know if it's safe to breathe. I wish you have boredom — real, spacious, unmonetized boredom — because boredom is where ideas are born. I wish you still have libraries, and that they are noisy with children. I wish you still know how to be alone without being lonely, and how to be together without being performative.

And if you don't remember us, that's okay. Most ancestors are forgotten as individuals. We don't remember the names of the people who invented the spoon or the song or the stitch that holds our clothes together, but we live inside their gifts anyway. If our time did anything useful for you, it will probably not be the grand speeches or the viral moments. It will be the quiet maintenance work: someone who kept a seed vault going, someone who taught a child to read with patience, someone who repaired a bridge instead of building a new one. Civilization is not mostly built from breakthroughs. It is built from upkeep.

Finally, if you can, look up tonight. Find a star. Remember that its light is old. Remember that you are standing on a rock made from the leftovers of other stars, thinking thoughts that no one else in the universe can think in quite the same way you can. That was true for us, too. It will be true for you. Some things don't change.

And if we could send one message forward that we hope you receive not as information but as permission, it is this: You get to be here too. Completely, stone-like, gloriously here. Don't waste too much of it somewhere else.

Thank you for carrying what we carried, for as long as you carry it. Put this down now and go drink some water. Go look out a window. The light at this hour has always been beautiful, no matter the century.
